title: 'Monkey Kong', garbled into 'Donkey'.
description:
'Monkey Kong', garbled into 'Donkey'. The legend says a blurred fax, or a bad phone line, turned 'Monkey' into 'Donkey' before anyone caught it. It is retold everywhere. There is no evidence for any version of it.

Asked to rescue a failed arcade game, he built Donkey Kong instead. He has said he chose 'donkey' from a dictionary to mean stubborn, and 'Kong' for a gorilla. At trial he added that in Japan 'King Kong' just meant any big, scary ape.

Nintendo has stolen King Kong, they say. Universal claimed Donkey Kong infringed its King Kong trademark. Awkwardly, seven years earlier Universal had gone to court to argue the opposite: that the King Kong story belonged to no one, and was in the public domain.

The two apes were not alike enough to confuse anyone. The court ruled for Nintendo in 1984 on a plain ground: no one would mistake a barrel-throwing cartoon for King Kong. Donkey Kong was, it wrote, 'at best... a parody'. Nintendo's lawyer was John Kirby.

The studio that owned King Kong had already told a court that King Kong belonged to everyone. It lost to the cartoon ape anyway.

Sources:
- https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/donkey-kong-mistranslation/ (Snopes, David Mikkelson, published 24 February 2001; read in full 27 August 2026): established that the popular legend that 'Donkey Kong' was a mistranslated, mistyped or misheard 'Monkey Kong' has no supporting evidence; that Shigeru Miyamoto, who built the 1981 game after being asked to salvage the failed arcade title 'Radarscope', has repeatedly said he used 'donkey' to convey stubbornness and 'Kong' to invoke a gorilla; that Miyamoto stated at the later Universal trial that 'King Kong' was treated in Japan as a generic term for a large, scary ape; and that Donkey Kong earned Nintendo of America about 100 million dollars in its first year.
- https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F2/746/112/30961/ (US Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, Universal City Studios, Inc. v. Nintendo Co., 746 F.2d 112, decided 4 October 1984; read in full 27 August 2026): established that Universal sued Nintendo in 1982 claiming Donkey Kong infringed and diluted its King Kong trademark; that Nintendo's counsel was John J. Kirby, Jr.; that the district court under Judge Sweet granted Nintendo summary judgment and the appeals court affirmed on the ground that there was no likelihood of consumer confusion, calling Donkey Kong 'at best... a parody of King Kong'; and, in footnote 1, that in a 1975 California case Universal had itself sought a declaration that it could remake King Kong because the story was in the public domain.
